title: Theorem 3.5 — On the Robustness of Kernel Ridge Regression Using the Cauchy Loss Function
text: Under certain regularity and boundedness assumptions, the clipped kernel ridge regression estimator achieves a convergence rate in squared L2 norm. The rate depends on the smoothness parameter alpha and the input dimension d. The result holds with high probability over the data distribution. The choices of regularization and kernel parameters are specified to attain this bound. Let Assumptions \ref {ass::logmoment}, \ref {ass::symmetry}, \ref {ass::decreasingtails}, and \ref {ass::Holder} hold, and suppose the true regression function $f^*$ is bounded by $M_0$, i.e., $\|f^*\|_{\infty } \leq M_0$. Furthermore, let the KCRR $\wideparen {f}_D$ be defined by \eqref {eq::KCRR}, using the clipping parameter $M = M_0$. Then, there exists a constant $c_1 > 0$ such that for any $q \in (0,1/2)$, by choosing \begin {align*} \lambda \asymp n^{-1}, \qquad \gamma \asymp n^{-\frac {1}{2\alpha +d}}, \qquad \sigma = 4 M_0 \vee c_1, \end {align*} we obtain \begin {align*} \|\wideparen {f}_D - f^*\|^2_{L_2(P_X)} \lesssim n^{-\frac {2\alpha }{(2\alpha +d)(1+q)}} \end {align*} with probability $P^n$ at least $1-1/n$.

title: TheoremSearch: Matched-noise training augmentation
text: Matched-noise training augmentation Training with noise is equivalent to adding a regularizer to the loss function. The regularizer is a designed function applied to the learning model. The loss function with noise approximates the original loss plus a constant times the regularizer. This relationship holds for the model parameters with and without noise. Given a symmetric sequence of object pairs, if the data augmentation policy equals the distribution derived from the Untied MixUp parameters, then the Untied MixUp loss equals the data augmentation training loss. Given a distribution of labeled examples with standard normal inputs, applying a specific augmentation algorithm produces a new distribution. For any real function and unit vector, the expected value of the function applied to the dot product under the augmented distribution equals the expected value of the noise-operator-transformed function under the original distribution. This holds provided the original expectation is finite. Training with Gaussian noise added to labels increases the output variance compared to training with original labels. The first term involves the noise variance and the eigenvalues of the kernel matrix. The second term involves the norm of the true function and the regularization parameter. A solution function is approximated using principal components from kernel PCA. The kernel is universal and has a spectral decomposition with decreasing eigenvalues. Boundedness conditions are assumed for the feature map and its tensor product. The projection of the solution onto the principal components converges to the true solution as the number of components increases. The generalization error in kernel ridge regression with a positive-definite kernel is asymptotically equivalent to the sum of squared target coefficients for eigenvalues below the ridge parameter. This holds under Gaussian assumptions on the eigenfunction evaluations and specific power-law decays for the eigenvalue density and target spectrum. The result applies in the limit of infinite data and vanishing ridge, with the ratio of ridge to the square root of the data size approaching zero. The error is given by an integral over small eigenvalues of the product of the reduced eigenvalue density and the expected squared coefficients. The optimal prediction equals the result from a linear ridge regression. This regression uses a specific noise variance and a transformed data matrix. The transformation involves scaling the original data by the square root of a covariance matrix. The formula expresses the prediction as a function of the transformed data and the observed outcomes.

title: Theorem F.1 (Theorem \ref {th:ridge} in the main text) — Locality defeats the curse of dimensionality in convolutional teacher-student scenarios
text: The generalization error in kernel ridge regression with a positive-definite kernel is asymptotically equivalent to the sum of squared target coefficients for eigenvalues below the ridge parameter. This holds under Gaussian assumptions on the eigenfunction evaluations and specific power-law decays for the eigenvalue density and target spectrum. The result applies in the limit of infinite data and vanishing ridge, with the ratio of ridge to the square root of the data size approaching zero. The error is given by an integral over small eigenvalues of the product of the reduced eigenvalue density and the expected squared coefficients. Let us consider a positive-definite kernel $K$ with eigenvalues $\Lambda _\rho $, $\sum _\rho \Lambda _\rho < \infty $, and eigenfunctions ${\Phi _\rho }$ learning a (random) target function $f^*$ in kernel ridge regression (\autoref {eq:argmin}) with ridge $\lambda $ from $P$ observations $f^*_{\mu }\,{=}\,f^*(\bm {x}^\mu )$, with $\bm {x}^\mu \in \mathbb {R}^d$ drawn from a certain probability distribution. Let us denote with $\mathcal {D}_T(\Lambda )$ the reduced density of kernel eigenvalues with respect to the target and $\epsilon (\lambda ,P)$ the generalisation error and also assume that \begin {itemize} \item [$i)$] For any $P$-tuple of indices $\rho _1,\dots ,\rho _P$, the vector $(\Phi _{\rho _1}(\bm {x}^1), \dots ,\Phi _{\rho _P}(\bm {x}^P))$ is a Gaussian random vector; \item [$ii)$] The target function can be written in the kernel eigenbasis with coefficients $c_\rho $ and $c^2(\Lambda _\rho )\,{=}\,\mathbb {E}[|c_\rho |^2]$, with $\mathcal {D}_T(\Lambda ) \sim \Lambda ^{-(1+r)}$, $c^2(\Lambda ) \sim \Lambda ^{q}$ asymptotically for small $\Lambda $ and $r\,{>}\,0$, $r\,{<}\,q\,{<}\,r\,{+}\,2$; \end {itemize} Then the following equivalence holds in the joint $P\to \infty $ and $\lambda \to 0$ limit with $1/(\lambda \sqrt {P})\to 0$: \begin {equation} \epsilon (\lambda , P) \sim \sum _{\left \lbrace \rho |\Lambda _\rho < \lambda \right \rbrace } \mathbb {E}{[|c_\rho |^2]} = \int _0^{\lambda } d\Lambda \mathcal {D}_T(\Lambda ) c^2(\Lambda ). \end {equation}
